title: Code Diffusion Models Are Continuous Human Noise Operators

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to test whether intermediate discrete representations produced during reverse code-diffusion resemble human mistakes, specifically investigating whether code diffusion acts as a "continuous human noise operator." No prior paper explicitly establishes or tests this empirical relationship between diffusion-generated errors and human-error operators. Papers like [2] and [15] discuss code diffusion models but focus on their generative capabilities or syntax tree operations, not their resemblance to human error patterns. Papers such as [24] and [26] address synthetic bug generation but do not explore diffusion models or their alignment with human mistakes. Thus, the purpose is **NONE**.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves analyzing pre-trained CodeFusion diffusion trajectories, measuring token changes and localization over time, and comparing diffusion-generated errors against human-error operators (BIFI, FLAME) and GPT-4o along dimensions like localization, diversity, and complexity. Paper [2] introduces CodeFusion, a pre-trained diffusion model for code generation, and discusses iterative denoising processes, which align with the mechanism's focus on diffusion trajectories. Paper [15] also describes neural diffusion models operating on syntax trees, which involve iterative refinement akin to the described mechanism. While neither paper explicitly compares diffusion errors to human-error operators, the underlying primitive of analyzing diffusion trajectories is substantively equivalent. Thus, the mechanism is **COVERED**.

### Evaluation
The evaluation design involves analyzing diffusion trajectories for fewer and more localized edits near the end of diffusion, as well as comparing diversity, complexity, and error patterns against existing generators and GPT-4o. Papers like [2], [15], and [27] evaluate code generation models using metrics such as diversity and complexity, which overlap with the evaluation design here. Paper [27] introduces CodeBERTScore for evaluating code generation, which aligns with the comparison of generated outputs against benchmarks. While the specific objects differ, the evaluation design (comparison of generated outputs along diversity, complexity, and error metrics) is substantively equivalent. Thus, the evaluation is **COVERED**.

### Domain
The domain is code generation and automated program repair. Papers [1], [2], [4], [5], [6], and [15] all operate within this general application area, addressing code generation, automated program repair, or related tasks. While the specific sub-problem of testing diffusion-generated errors against human-error operators is new, the broader domain of code generation and repair is well-covered. Thus, the domain is **COVERED**.

## Purpose

The purpose is: "Directly use a pre-trained code diffusion model for last-mile repair of broken code without training a specialized repair system."

This combines two elements: (1) using a pre-trained model without task-specific training, and (2) applying it to code repair. Paper [13] (CodeFusion) is a pre-trained diffusion model for code generation, but its purpose is generation, not repair. Paper [18] (DDRM) addresses using pre-trained diffusion models for image restoration without problem-specific training — "efficient solutions often require problem-specific supervised training... whereas unsupervised methods... not problem-specific." This is structurally equivalent: use a pre-trained diffusion model for restoration without training a specialized system. However, the domain is image, not code. The purpose-level objective — "apply a pre-trained diffusion model to fix corrupted inputs without retraining" — is covered by [18]. Papers [3], [9], [10], [17] address APR but require training specialized systems. Paper [26] (SDEdit) also uses a pre-trained diffusion model for editing without retraining. The closest match at the problem-class level is [18] or [26]: use pre-trained diffusion model for restoration without specialized training. I'll note [18] and [26] as covering this purpose.

## Mechanism

The mechanism is: "Inject broken code by adding noise to it and resuming the reverse diffusion process (noise-then-denoise); choose noise level via any%/best%/vote% strategies."

Paper [26] (SDEdit) introduces exactly this primitive: add noise to a user input (stroke painting) and then run the reverse diffusion process to get a realistic image — "synthesize realistic images by first adding noise to the input... then denoising." This is the same "add noise, then denoise" mechanism. Paper [5] (Resfusion) also modifies the starting point of diffusion for restoration. Paper [18] (DDRM) uses pre-trained diffusion for restoration but via a different mechanism (pseudo-inverse). The any%/best%/vote% strategies are selection heuristics on top of the core mechanism. The core primitive — add noise to a corrupted input and resume reverse diffusion — is clearly covered by [26] (SDEdit).

## Evaluation

The evaluation involves: repair rate percentages on Python/Excel snippets, comparison against baselines (Codex, BIFI, LaMirage, GPT-4o/RING), across noise levels.

Papers [1], [3], [9], [16], [19] all use benchmark-based evaluation of program repair with metrics like patch correctness rate, comparison against LLM baselines. Paper [16] (RepairBench) uses execution-based evaluation comparing frontier models. Paper [19] (Benchmarking Educational Program Repair) benchmarks repair across datasets with standard metrics. Paper [3] (CIRCLE) compares against baselines across programming languages. The evaluation design — measure repair success rate on code snippets, compare against LLM and specialized system baselines — is standard in APR evaluation and appears in [3], [9], [16], [19].

## Domain

The domain is automated program repair (last-mile repair of broken code).

Papers [1], [3], [9], [10], [16], [17], [19] all work in automated program repair. This is clearly covered.
